assistant.content: Of course. Proportional reinsurance is sharing risk by insured amount, such as quota share reinsurance (ceding premiums and losses by a fixed percentage) and surplus reinsurance (ceding the portion above the retention proportionally). Non-proportional reinsurance is sharing by loss amount, such as excess of loss reinsurance (the part above the agreed deductible is borne by the reinsurer) and stop-loss reinsurance (triggered when the annual loss ratio exceeds a threshold). Simply put: proportional is 'cutting the cake', non-proportional is 'guarding against catastrophe'.

user.content: Mhm, that analogy is good. Can you give a practical example? For instance, a case from auto insurance or property insurance, to help me understand it better.

assistant.content: Okay. Suppose the primary insurer underwrites a car insurance policy with a sum insured of 500,000 yuan and a retention of 200,000 yuan. Under quota share reinsurance with a 50% cession, 250,000 yuan would be ceded; under surplus reinsurance, the portion exceeding 200,000 yuan (300,000 yuan) would be fully ceded. This is proportional reinsurance. Non-proportional reinsurance, such as per-risk excess of loss: assume the deductible for each accident is set at 100,000 yuan; if the loss is 250,000 yuan, the excess of 150,000 yuan is borne by the reinsurer. It is suitable for frequent small losses. You can use the logic framework 'proportional shares the amount insured, non-proportional shares the loss' to remember.

user.content: I understand. Proportional means both premiums and claims are shared proportionally, while non-proportional only looks at whether claims exceed the threshold. So 'stop-loss' reinsurance is non-proportional, right? This was mentioned in my practice errors.

assistant.content: Correct. Stop-loss reinsurance (loss ratio excess of loss) is indeed a type of non-proportional reinsurance. It sets a threshold based on the overall loss ratio within a year; for example, the portion of the loss ratio exceeding 80% is borne by the reinsurer. It is often used to guard against accumulation risk.
